title: Fidaxomicin: C. difficile Treatment, Not a General Macrolide
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Fidaxomicin is an oral antibacterial used specifically for C. difficile-associated diarrhea; it is not a systemic treatment for pneumonia, bacteremia, or other routine infections. Safe care includes hydration/status monitoring, recurrence recognition, allergy surveillance, and infection-control reinforcement.
recognize: Persistent profuse diarrhea, abdominal distention, fever, hypotension, or ileus can signal severe or fulminant disease rather than a simple medication side effect.
A history of macrolide allergy may increase hypersensitivity concern even though fidaxomicin has minimal systemic absorption.
priorities: Assess stool pattern, hydration, abdominal findings, hemodynamics, and severity/recurrence cues.
Escalate ileus, toxic megacolon concern, severe dehydration, hypotension, or hypersensitivity.
assessMonitor: Trend stool frequency, abdominal pain/distention, hydration, renal function when clinically indicated, and recurrence after treatment.
interventions: Administer the full prescribed course and maintain C. difficile transmission precautions/environmental cleaning according to facility policy.
medicationSafety: Use only for proven or strongly suspected C. difficile infection, not as a broad systemic antibiotic.
Do not mask worsening ileus or severe colitis with reflex antimotility therapy.
teaching: Finish treatment and seek care if diarrhea returns after therapy or severe abdominal swelling/pain develops.
delegationScope: Administration and stool/hydration monitoring may be within PN scope; severe colitis assessment requires escalation.
examTrap: Choosing fidaxomicin to treat a bloodstream infection because it is called a macrolide antibacterial.
oneLinePearl: Fidaxomicin stays in the gut—think C. difficile, not systemic infection.

title: Oral Vancomycin: Route Determines the Infection It Treats
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Oral vancomycin is used for C. difficile-associated diarrhea and selected enterocolitis because the drug acts in the gastrointestinal tract. Oral capsules do not provide reliable systemic therapy for bacteremia, pneumonia, endocarditis, or other invasive infections.
recognize: Route is a pharmacologic decision: IV vancomycin treats systemic susceptible infections, while oral vancomycin is intentionally gut-directed.
Systemic absorption can increase in severe colitis or renal dysfunction, so nephrotoxicity/ototoxicity still deserve attention in susceptible patients.
priorities: Verify indication and route before administration.
Assess diarrhea severity, hydration, renal risk, and concomitant nephrotoxic/ototoxic drugs.
Escalate severe colitis, major renal decline, hearing changes, or systemic infection being treated with the wrong route.
assessMonitor: Trend stool pattern, hydration, renal function in higher-risk patients, hearing symptoms, and clinical response.
interventions: Administer orally as ordered and continue C. difficile infection-control measures.
medicationSafety: Do not substitute oral capsules for IV vancomycin when systemic exposure is required.
Current labeling warns that oral systemic absorption can occur in some patients.
redFlags: Bacteremia/sepsis signs while receiving oral-only therapy for a systemic infection
teaching: The same drug name can treat different infections depending on route; do not switch formulations on your own.
delegationScope: Administration and symptom monitoring may be within PN scope; route/indication mismatch requires immediate pharmacist/RN/provider clarification.
examTrap: Giving oral vancomycin for MRSA bacteremia because vancomycin is active against MRSA.
oneLinePearl: For vancomycin, route is part of the diagnosis: oral treats the gut; IV reaches systemic infection.
sourceBasis: DailyMed vancomycin hydrochloride capsule labeling updated 2026-03 to 2026-06

title: Entecavir: Chronic Hepatitis B and the Danger of Abrupt Stopping
bottomLine: Entecavir suppresses hepatitis B virus but does not eradicate chronic HBV. Stopping therapy can trigger a severe hepatitis flare; HIV status matters because entecavir is not an adequate HIV regimen and can select HIV resistance when HIV is untreated.
recognize: Jaundice, dark urine, severe fatigue, abdominal swelling, or rising liver tests after discontinuation can signal HBV exacerbation.
Lactic acidosis/hepatomegaly is uncommon but serious.
priorities: Verify HBV and HIV status, renal function, adherence, and whether the medication has been interrupted.
Escalate hepatic decompensation, severe post-discontinuation flare, or lactic-acidosis symptoms.
assessMonitor: Trend HBV DNA/liver tests as ordered, renal function, adherence, and clinical signs of hepatic decompensation.
interventions: Administer consistently and coordinate any planned discontinuation with the HBV care team and post-treatment monitoring plan.
medicationSafety: Current U.S. labeling carries boxed warnings for severe acute HBV exacerbation after stopping, HIV/HBV coinfection concerns, and lactic acidosis/hepatomegaly.
Dose selection depends on renal function and treatment history.
redFlags: Severe weakness/tachypnea suggestive of lactic acidosis
teaching: Do not stop entecavir because you feel well; viral suppression requires ongoing follow-up and stopping can worsen hepatitis.
delegationScope: Routine administration and adherence reinforcement may be within PN scope; antiviral selection/discontinuation requires provider management.
examTrap: Stopping entecavir when HBV DNA becomes undetectable without a clinician-directed monitoring plan.
oneLinePearl: Entecavir suppresses HBV; stopping can wake it up dangerously.

title: Sofosbuvir/Velpatasvir: Hepatitis C Cure With HBV and Interaction Checks
bottomLine: Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir is a direct-acting antiviral combination used for hepatitis C. Before and during therapy, the major nursing safety issues are hepatitis B reactivation, adherence, acid-reducing and other drug interactions, liver status, and serious bradycardia risk with amiodarone-containing combinations.
recognize: HBV can reactivate during or after HCV direct-acting antiviral treatment.
Acid-reducing medicines can lower velpatasvir exposure depending on product and timing.
priorities: Review HBV testing, medication list including acid suppressants/amiodarone, liver status, and adherence.
Escalate jaundice, hepatic decompensation, symptomatic bradycardia, or suspected treatment interruption/failure.
assessMonitor: Trend HCV virologic follow-up, liver status, HBV monitoring when indicated, heart rate if relevant, and medication interactions.
interventions: Administer exactly as prescribed and use product-specific instructions for antacids/H2 blockers/PPIs.
medicationSafety: Current labeling carries a boxed warning for HBV reactivation in HCV/HBV coinfection.
Amiodarone with sofosbuvir-containing regimens has been associated with serious symptomatic bradycardia.
teaching: Bring all acid-reducing medicines, supplements, and heart medications to review before starting treatment.
delegationScope: Administration and interaction screening may be within PN role; HCV regimen selection and treatment-failure interpretation require specialist/provider management.
examTrap: Giving a proton-pump inhibitor at any time with sofosbuvir/velpatasvir without checking product-specific interaction instructions.
oneLinePearl: HCV therapy can cure infection—but first check HBV and every interacting medication.

title: Topical Mupirocin: Match the Product to the Site
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Topical mupirocin is used for selected superficial bacterial skin infections such as impetigo. Product formulation and site matter: standard topical products should not be treated as interchangeable with intranasal preparations or used in the eyes or other mucosal sites unless that exact product is intended for it.
recognize: Worsening spreading erythema, fever, abscess, lymphangitis, or systemic illness suggests deeper infection/source-control needs rather than simply more ointment.
Local burning or dermatitis may indicate irritation or allergy.
priorities: Confirm the exact product, infection site, wound depth, and signs of systemic/deeper infection.
Escalate rapidly spreading cellulitis, abscess, fever, necrosis, or severe local reaction.
assessMonitor: Trend lesion size, drainage, pain, surrounding erythema, systemic symptoms, and local skin reaction.
interventions: Apply only to the prescribed site using clean technique and complete the prescribed course.
medicationSafety: Current topical labeling states it is not for ophthalmic or intranasal/mucosal use unless a specifically indicated formulation is used.
Avoid prolonged unnecessary use that promotes resistance.
teaching: Use only on the ordered skin area and seek reassessment if the infection spreads or fails to improve.
delegationScope: Topical administration may be within PN scope; assessment of worsening infection requires licensed clinical judgment.
examTrap: Using topical skin mupirocin inside the eye because the infection is near the eyelid.
oneLinePearl: Mupirocin is product-and-site specific—skin ointment is not an all-purpose antibiotic paste.

title: Permethrin: Treat the Infestation and the Exposure Network
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Permethrin is used topically for scabies and lice in product-specific formulations. Successful treatment requires correct application time/site, repeat treatment when indicated, evaluation of close contacts, and environmental measures appropriate to the infestation—not repeated overapplication for persistent post-treatment itching alone.
recognize: Itching can persist after successful scabies treatment because inflammation resolves slowly.
New burrows/live mites or continuing household spread is more suggestive of treatment failure or reinfestation.
priorities: Identify whether the product is for scabies or lice and follow the exact age/site/application instructions.
Assess household/close-contact exposure and signs of secondary bacterial infection.
assessMonitor: Trend new lesions/burrows, live lice/mites, itching trajectory, skin irritation, and recurrence among contacts.
interventions: Coordinate contact treatment and laundering/environmental steps according to current public-health/product guidance.
medicationSafety: Do not repeatedly reapply because itching persists without evidence of active infestation.
Avoid eyes/mucous membranes and use only the formulation/site directed.
redFlags: Crusted scabies in an immunocompromised patient
teaching: Persistent itch does not automatically mean treatment failed; look for new active lesions and follow the repeat-treatment schedule exactly.
delegationScope: Application/teaching may be within PN scope; outbreak/public-health procedures vary by setting and jurisdiction.
examTrap: Reapplying permethrin every day until all itching stops.
oneLinePearl: Treat the parasite, contacts, and environment—not the itch alone.

title: Oral Terbinafine: Fungal Therapy With Liver and Sensory Monitoring
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Oral terbinafine is a systemic antifungal used for selected dermatophyte infections such as onychomycosis. Hepatic injury, important drug interactions, and taste/smell disturbances are key safety issues; nail appearance improves slowly even after fungal eradication.
recognize: Jaundice, dark urine, persistent nausea, right-upper-quadrant discomfort, or profound fatigue can signal hepatic injury.
Taste or smell disturbance can reduce intake and occasionally persist.
priorities: Review liver disease, baseline/ordered hepatic testing, medication interactions, and whether the diagnosis truly requires systemic antifungal therapy.
Escalate hepatic symptoms, severe rash, neutropenic infection symptoms, or major taste/smell changes affecting nutrition.
assessMonitor: Trend liver-related symptoms/labs when ordered, rash, CBC if clinically indicated, intake/weight, and treatment response.
interventions: Administer the full prescribed course and reinforce that healthy nail growth takes months.
medicationSafety: Avoid casual systemic use in active/chronic liver disease without prescriber evaluation.
Review CYP-mediated interactions and duplicate antifungal therapy.
teaching: Report liver symptoms or major taste/smell changes and do not expect a damaged nail to look normal immediately after treatment.
delegationScope: Administration and symptom monitoring may be within PN scope; systemic-antifungal selection requires prescriber management.
examTrap: Stopping oral terbinafine because the nail still looks abnormal after a short period despite clinical improvement.
oneLinePearl: Terbinafine kills fungus faster than a nail can grow—watch the liver while you wait.

title: Benzathine Penicillin G: Deep IM Only, Never IV
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Benzathine penicillin G is a long-acting intramuscular penicillin used for selected infections including syphilis. The route is a critical safety issue: this formulation is for deep IM administration and must never be given intravenously because severe neurologic/cardiopulmonary injury and death can occur.
recognize: Syphilis treatment depends on disease stage, pregnancy, and neurologic/ocular involvement; benzathine penicillin is not automatically the correct formulation for every manifestation.
Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction can cause acute fever/chills after syphilis therapy and must be distinguished from anaphylaxis.
priorities: Verify exact penicillin formulation, indication/stage, allergy history, route, pregnancy status, and whether neuro/ocular disease requires different management.
Observe for anaphylaxis and escalate neurologic/cardiopulmonary symptoms immediately.
assessMonitor: Monitor injection reaction, allergy/anaphylaxis, symptom response, and follow-up serology per the treatment plan.
interventions: Administer by the approved deep-IM technique only when authorized and ensure emergency allergy treatment is available.
medicationSafety: Never administer benzathine penicillin G intravenously or confuse it with aqueous penicillin G products.
Product selection and syphilis regimen depend on the clinical syndrome.
teaching: Complete follow-up testing and partner/public-health steps as directed; fever after treatment should still be reported so reaction versus allergy can be assessed.
delegationScope: IM administration authority varies by state/facility; STI diagnosis/staging and public-health actions require authorized clinician/system processes.
examTrap: Giving benzathine penicillin G IV because another penicillin G formulation can be given intravenously.
oneLinePearl: Benzathine penicillin G is a formulation where route can be fatal: deep IM only.
sourceBasis: DailyMed Bicillin L-A/benzathine penicillin G labeling current 2026

title: Ceftriaxone: Broad Utility, But Site, Allergy, and Calcium Matter
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Ceftriaxone is a third-generation cephalosporin used for many susceptible infections, including selected meningitis, sepsis, pneumonia, and STI regimens. Safe use requires correct indication, beta-lactam allergy assessment, neonatal/calcium precautions, biliary effects, and culture-guided de-escalation.
recognize: A vague childhood 'penicillin allergy' is not the same as a documented severe immediate beta-lactam reaction.
Neonates have special bilirubin and IV-calcium safety restrictions that do not apply identically to older patients.
priorities: Verify indication, allergy phenotype, cultures when ordered, age/neonatal status, IV-calcium exposure, and hepatic/biliary symptoms.
Escalate anaphylaxis, severe diarrhea/C. difficile concern, hemolysis, or significant biliary complications.
assessMonitor: Trend temperature/infection response, cultures, CBC, renal/hepatic context, diarrhea, and allergy signs.
interventions: Administer on schedule and support stewardship by narrowing therapy when culture/clinical data allow.
medicationSafety: Do not mix or coadminister incompatibly with calcium-containing IV solutions in neonates; follow current label/facility compatibility rules.
Avoid hard-coded STI dosing outside the current CDC regimen/order.
teaching: Report severe diarrhea, rash, breathing difficulty, or right-upper-quadrant pain; finish the prescribed regimen.
delegationScope: Parenteral antibiotic administration authority varies by state/facility; allergy assessment and neonatal compatibility concerns require licensed clinical judgment.
examTrap: Assuming every penicillin-allergic patient can never receive ceftriaxone without clarifying the reaction history.
oneLinePearl: Ceftriaxone is versatile—but age, allergy phenotype, calcium, and infection site still decide safety.

title: Daptomycin: Gram-Positive Power, But Not for Pneumonia
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Daptomycin is an IV lipopeptide used for selected serious gram-positive infections such as bacteremia/right-sided endocarditis or complicated skin infections. It is not used to treat pneumonia because pulmonary surfactant inactivates its antibacterial activity; muscle toxicity and eosinophilic pneumonia are major safety concerns.
recognize: New muscle pain/weakness with CK elevation can indicate myopathy or rhabdomyolysis.
New fever, dyspnea, hypoxemia, and infiltrates after exposure can signal eosinophilic pneumonia.
priorities: Verify infection site, cultures, renal function, baseline/ordered CK, and concurrent statin or other myotoxic therapy.
Escalate severe muscle symptoms, major CK rise, renal deterioration, or new pulmonary syndrome.
assessMonitor: Trend CK, renal function, muscle symptoms, respiratory status, cultures, and treatment response.
interventions: Administer according to product/facility infusion instructions and preserve culture-guided stewardship.
medicationSafety: Do not use for pneumonia despite gram-positive susceptibility because lung surfactant inactivates the drug.
Renal impairment affects dosing interval and toxicity monitoring.
complications: Treatment failure if used for pneumonia
teaching: Report new muscle pain/weakness or new breathing problems promptly.
delegationScope: IV administration authority varies by state/facility; infection-site selection and toxicity interpretation require RN/provider/pharmacist collaboration.
examTrap: Choosing daptomycin for MRSA pneumonia because the organism is susceptible in vitro.
oneLinePearl: Daptomycin can treat bloodstream MRSA—but lung surfactant makes pneumonia the wrong target.
